title: Job 17:10–16
context: Job closes his reply by inviting his friends to come back and try again, though he expects to find no wise man among them. His days are past and his plans broken off. He says that they change night into day, claiming the light is near in the presence of darkness, which many interpreters take as Job’s rejection of the friends’ easy promises of restoration (compare Job 11:17). He then speaks of Sheol, the place of the dead, as his house, of making his bed in darkness, and of calling corruption his father and the worm his mother and sister, before asking where his hope is and whether it will go down with him to the gates of Sheol and into the dust. The speech ends with that question unanswered. These are Job’s words in the depth of grief, and the book lets them stand without immediate resolution; the LORD’s speeches and the ending come later (Job 38:1; 42:7). Arminian and Reformed readers generally read the passage as honest lament that Scripture includes and does not rush to correct, much like Psalm 88.

verses.text: But as for you all, come back. I will not find a wise man among you.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see Job inviting his friends to come back and try again, though he expects to find no wise man among them. He has little hope in their counsel.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see Job’s frustration with the friends’ arguments. Both traditions commonly read the verse within the dialogue, leaving the final verdict to the LORD (Job 42:7).

verses.text: My days are past. My plans are broken off, as are the thoughts of my heart.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see Job saying his days are past and his plans and heart’s desires are broken off. His future seems gone.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see an honest expression of shattered hopes. Readers in both traditions commonly read the verse as lament, letting its sorrow stand.

verses.text: They change the night into day, saying ‘The light is near’ in the presence of darkness.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see Job saying they change night into day, calling light near in darkness. Many take this as rejecting the friends’ easy promises of restoration.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see Job resisting comfort that ignores his real condition (compare Job 11:17). Both traditions commonly read the verse as a caution against offering hope that dismisses present pain.

verses.text: If I look for Sheol as my house, if I have spread my couch in the darkness,
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see Job speaking of Sheol, the place of the dead, as his house and of making his bed in darkness. Death seems to be his only prospect.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the language of one who expects to die (compare Psalm 88:3). Readers in both traditions commonly let the verse speak as Job’s lament without adding a lecture on the afterlife.

verses.text: if I have said to corruption, ‘You are my father,’ and to the worm, ‘My mother,’ and ‘My sister,’
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see Job calling corruption his father and the worm his mother and sister. Decay has become his closest family.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see stark imagery of death and the grave. Both traditions commonly read the verse as part of Job’s honest lament, handled as the text gives it.

verses.text: where then is my hope? As for my hope, who will see it?
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see Job asking where his hope is and who will see it. The question expresses deep despair and is left hanging.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see Job’s question left open in the dialogue. Readers in both traditions commonly read it as honest lament, with the book’s later answer still to come (Job 38:1).

verses.text: Shall it go down with me to the gates of Sheol, or descend together into the dust?”
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see Job asking whether his hope will go down with him to the gates of Sheol and into the dust. The speech ends with a question.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the chapter close in darkness. Both traditions commonly read the verse as lament that Scripture includes without immediate resolution (compare Isaiah 38:10).
